Leaves change colour in autumn because trees prepare for winter by breaking down chlorophyll and sealing off their leaves. 
The Main Triggers
  • Shorter Days and Less Sunlight: As autumn arrives, nights grow longer and daylight decreases. This signals the tree to stop making chlorophyll—the green pigment it uses to make food through photosynthesis.
  • Cooler Temperatures: Drop in temperature accelerates the breakdown of chlorophyll, causing the vibrant green color to fade. 
Where the Colors Come From
  • Yellows and Oranges (Carotenoids): These pigments are present in the leaf all summer long, hidden by the heavy green of chlorophyll. Once the green chlorophyll breaks down, the yellow xanthophylls and orange carotenoids become visible. 
  • Reds and Purples (Anthocyanins): Unlike yellows, these colors are made fresh in autumn. As sugars get trapped in the leaf after fluid movement slows down, the tree produces new pigments called anthocyanins. Sunny days and cool, crisp nights help boost red and purple shades. 
  • Browns: When chlorophyll, carotenoids, and anthocyanins all break down completely, what remains are cell walls and waste products, leaving the leaf a dry brown. 
Why Leaves Fall
Once the leaf stops functioning, the tree forms a special separation layer (the abscission layer) at the base of the stem. It cuts off the flow of water and nutrients to the leaf, letting it drop to the ground so the tree can survive the cold and dry conditions of winter. 
You can read more about the science behind this seasonal shift on the Smithsonian Institution Story Page or through the Forestry England Guide. 
If you'd like, I can explain why cold nights make reds brighter or discuss how climate change affects autumn leaves.
